QF.id: SIA Social Stock Exchange Introduction and Instruments_16

question.text: Chapter 2 references a 'starvation cycle' affecting NPOs in India. Which of the following BEST describes this cycle?

answer.text: NPOs over-invest in non-programmatic overhead, starving beneficiaries of program funds.
Retail donors redirect funds through CSR only, starving small NPOs of direct public donations.
Government grants are released late in the fiscal year, starving NPOs of liquidity during the operational months.

Donations from institutional sources are typically restricted to program costs, forcing NPOs to absorb non-program costs (rent, utilities, staff training, research) from internal resources, which constrains their investment in organisational infrastructure and impedes growth.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Section 2.2.2(A), institutional donations are 'typically permitted to be spent only towards programs, as a safeguard against their misuse. Non-program costs such as rent, utilities, staff training, research, etc. have to be borne by NPOs from internal resources. This has produced the so-called 'starvation cycle', constraining NPOs' ability to invest in essential organisational infrastructure and impeding their growth.' The SSE partly addresses this by enabling donation routing that permits organisational build-out. The Trap: Option A inverts cause and effect. Option C is a real issue but not the 'starvation cycle' as defined. Option D describes a liquidity problem, not the structural funding restriction the text identifies. Cross-Exam Context: V-A (MF Distributor) touches CSR donor-side. X-A/X-B (IA) touches HNI donor-advised-giving; the 'starvation cycle' is XXIII-specific. Assessor's Pro-Tip: When measuring organisational capacity under SAS-100, benchmark the NPO's overhead-to-programme ratio against peer-comparable NPOs (GiveIndia publishes such ratios) — a ratio below the peer median may indicate starvation-cycle under-investment rather than operational excellence.
